In 1948, at a symposium in Pasadena, the mathematician John von Neumann asked a question that sounds like an engineering puzzle and turns out to be a question about life. Could a machine build a copy of itself? The difficulty is a regress. To build a copy, the machine needs a description of itself. But the description is part of the machine, so it must contain a description of the description, and so on forever. Von Neumann's way out was to use one description in two different ways. A constructor reads the description and builds what it specifies. A copier duplicates the description blindly, without interpreting it. Build the offspring from the instructions, copy the instructions without reading them, hand the copy over, and the regress disappears. And if the copying is occasionally imperfect, the offspring differ, which supplies the variation evolution needs. This was five years before Watson and Crick described the double helix, yet it closely parallels how cells use DNA. Genes are read, transcribed, and translated to build proteins, and the same DNA is copied, base by base, without being interpreted, to make a new cell. von Neumann had worked out the logical architecture of life from first principles. This episode makes the strongest case I can for one claim and then tests it. The claim is that life, intelligence, and computation are a single continuum. It has four steps. First, replicators arise naturally wherever computation and interaction meet. leaps in complexity come from merging. Third, anything that keeps itself going must regulate, and good regulation requires a model of what is being regulated, which makes prediction the core of being alive. Fourth, the hardest things to predict are other predictors, so minds grew by modeling other minds. The most ambitious recent statement of this view is a 2025 book by Blaise Aguera e.
